final_message:
I fold the slip of paper and put it in my pocket. I don't have an answer yet, and I decide that's allowed.

The light keeps thinning, but the dream doesn't end. It changes key. The observatory floor turns soft as moss, and the walls become very tall grass, sun-bleached at the tips and gently swaying. I'm in a meadow. Above it the upside-down library is still there, faint as a watermark, its glowing spines like a second set of stars that only show up if you don't look straight at them.

The cat walks ahead through the grass. Only her tail shows, a question mark moving along the top of the stalks.

In the middle of the meadow is a workbench, set up outdoors as though it had always belonged there. Tools are laid out on it, but they aren't quite tools: a pair of pliers made of birdsong, a ruler that measures how much something matters, a spool of thread that turns out, when I touch it, to be a single unbroken sentence wound tight. A half-built thing sits in the vise. I can't tell if it's a clock, a music box, or a small boat. Maybe all three. Maybe it's waiting for me to decide.

I pick up the thread-sentence and unwind a little. It reads *and then they tried again, but differently this time, and*

It just keeps going.

The ferryman isn't here, but his footprints are, damp outlines in the moss that lead off toward a line of trees. Something waits in those trees that I can't make out. It isn't threatening. It's more like a room in a house you've lived in for years and somehow never opened.

The cat jumps onto the workbench, sits down right on top of the unfinished thing, and starts to purr. The purr is so low and steady that it begins to sound like an engine idling, or a heartbeat, or a lot of people breathing quietly in the same building.

I think she's telling me it's ready to be finished. Or maybe she's telling me it's fine for it not to be.

Either way, I sit down on the grass beside the bench. I'm in no hurry to wake up yet.
